source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Jonas_2014_PharmacotherapyAUD_MA.pdf, the version of record, JAMA 2014;311(18):1889–1900. All 12 pages were read in a -layout text extraction: abstract, methods, results, discussion, limitations, conclusions, article information and references. Table 1 (p. 1892), Figure 2 (p. 1893), Figure 3 (p. 1894) and the text of pp. 1895 and 1897 were checked on pages rendered at 200 dpi; all pages were viewed at 110 dpi. The forest-plot rows of Figures 2 and 3 were re-added by script to check the crude totals, the participant numbers and the trial durations. The online Supplement (eTables 1–7, eFigures 1–10), the AHRQ technical report and the editorial were not read.

claims.overstatement: None in what the claim takes from this source. It uses the review's association wording, keeps the null result in the low-risk trials and quotes the authors' own list of explanations. The quoted phrase matches p. 1897 exactly.
claims.note: Not supported by this source, which contradicts it: 'more people stopped because of side effects (risk ratio 1.35, 1.01 to 1.80)' (taken from the Cochrane review). This review found no significant difference in withdrawal from trials because of adverse events for acamprosate (Results › Adverse Effects, p. 1895; abstract, p. 1889). The claim should give both reviews' results. Everything the claim takes from Jonas checks on the rendered pages: return to any drinking RD −0.09 (−0.14 to −0.04), 16 trials, 4,847 people, I² 80.8%, NNT 12 (8 to 26), moderate strength (Table 1; Figure 2). Crude totals recomputed from the 16 rows of Figure 2, same as the claim: 1968/2576 = 76.4% against 1893/2271 = 83.4%, and 2576 + 2271 = 4847. Risk-of-bias subgroups: high/unclear −0.13 (3 trials, 757), medium −0.11 (12, 3438), low −0.02 (−0.09 to 0.05; 4, 1409) (pp. 1893–1894). The four low-risk trials in Figure 2 add up to 1409 (COMBINE 612, Mason 2006 601, Morley 2006 116, Kiefer 2003 80). COMBINE and Mason 2006 hold 1066 of the four trials' 1227 events, and both are US trials (p. 1897). Mason 2006's point estimate favours placebo (+0.04, 0.00 to 0.08). 'The other 15 trials' are the review's 15 at medium, high or unclear risk: the vast majority European, 1 US and 1 Brazilian, typically recruited from inpatient settings or treatment programmes (p. 1897). Also consistent: return to heavy drinking −0.01 (−0.04 to 0.03), 7 trials; percentage of drinking days −8.8; deaths 7 against 6. Reading caution for the editor: the crude difference is 7.0 per 100, smaller than the pooled 9. With I² 80.8%, random-effects weighting gives the two large US trials 16% of the weight although they hold 25% of the participants (editors' arithmetic from Figure 2 weights). Suggested additions from this source: acamprosate's other significant harms here, anxiety (NNH 7, 5 to 11; 2 trials, 624 people) and vomiting (NNH 42; 4 trials). Jonas's diarrhoea NNH of 11 (6 to 34; 12 trials) is about 9 more per 100, consistent with the claim's Cochrane figure. On the head-to-head sentence: in this review's matching pool (3 trials, 800 people; RD 0.02, −0.03 to 0.08), COMBINE supplies 612 people (77%), and its naltrexone arm is the review's higher-dose group (editors' arithmetic from Figure 2). Funding and interests as in the claim: AHRQ contract; no conflicts reported. AHRQ staff reviewed drafts and had to approve submission (p. 1897).

claims.overstatement: None for the parts from this source. 'Was associated with' matches the review's wording for nalmefene.
claims.note: Checked on the renders, all the same as the claim: nalmefene heavy drinking days per month WMD −2.0 (−3.0 to −1.0; 2 trials, n = 806); drinks per drinking day −1.02 (−1.77 to −0.28; 3 trials, n = 608); withdrawal from trials because of adverse events NNH 12 (7 to 50; 5 trials, n = 2054), i.e. about 1 more in 12 (p. 1895). The disulfiram sentence matches pp. 1895–1896: no disulfiram trial evaluated supervised administration, which the authors say may underestimate its benefit in supervised programmes. This review's own disulfiram result (RD −0.04, −0.11 to 0.03; 2 trials; low) agrees with the claim. Qualifiers the claim could use. (1) For injectable naltrexone this review pools the same 2 trials with the same numbers (939 and 615 people) as the claim gives for the 2023 review, which supports 'shares most of its trials'. It also found fewer heavy drinking days (WMD −4.6, −8.5 to −0.56; 2 trials, n = 926; low), partly on data from a personal communication (Table 1, footnote e); the claim is silent on this. (2) Valproic acid was associated with less return to heavy drinking in 2 small trials, one in people with bipolar disorder (Figure 3: RD −0.32, −0.52 to −0.11); the claim does not mention it, consistent with its rule of reporting only the 2023 review's medicines. (3) Nalmefene's specific harms here were dizziness (NNH 7), nausea (7), insomnia (10), vomiting (17) and headache (26). (4) For topiramate the 2014 estimates point the same way as the 2023 figures the claim gives: % heavy drinking days −9.0 (3 trials, 691); cognitive dysfunction NNH 12; paraesthesias NNH 4; taste abnormalities NNH 7. Gabapentin had a single trial in 2014 (p. 1891), and baclofen results are only in the Supplement, so the 2014 review gives no printed estimate for either. The review's last author is first author of the larger injectable-naltrexone trial (ref 44, 62% of that pool's weight); the conflict statement reports none. The claim contains no dose or regimen.

claims.overstatement: None in the sentence drawn from this source.
claims.note: The closing sentence matches p. 1891: most trials included psychosocial co-interventions, so the effect sizes are the added benefit of medication beyond psychosocial treatment and placebo. The Limitations add that the variety of co-interventions limits certainty about medicines used alone or added to a particular psychosocial treatment, and that medicines were not compared with psychosocial treatments (p. 1897). Also consistent with the claim: COMBINE randomized 1383 treatment-seeking patients, including a behavioural-intervention-only group without pills (p. 1891). Its medical management was up to 9 manual-guided visits (weeks 0, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 16), about 45 minutes and then about 20 minutes each, with encouragement to attend community support groups (p. 1896); this supports 'nine brief medical-support visits', which strictly means up to nine. A qualifier for the editor: this review summarizes COMBINE (p. 1894) as finding better drinking outcomes than placebo with naltrexone, the behavioural intervention or both. That is the trial's own framing, and it fits the claim's good-clinical-outcome figures (71 against 58 in 100). But it reads more favourably to the therapy than the claim's headline, which concerns the therapy's main effect averaged over the pill groups, a comparison this review does not report. The review also notes a small, not clinically meaningful quality-of-life gain with naltrexone plus the behavioural intervention (p. 1895).

anchors.extracted: Studies typically included psychosocial co-interventions, so pooled effect sizes are the added benefit of medication beyond psychosocial interventions and placebo. Medications were not compared with psychosocial treatments, and the variety of co-interventions limits certainty about benefit when medicines are used alone or with a particular psychosocial treatment.

anchors.extracted: COMBINE: 1383 treatment-seeking patients randomized to medical management with naltrexone, acamprosate, both or two placebos, with or without the combined behavioural intervention, or to the behavioural intervention alone without pills. The review summarizes COMBINE as finding better drinking outcomes than placebo with naltrexone, the behavioural intervention or both, and no efficacy for acamprosate. claims.overstatement: Mild. 'Reduced return to heavy drinking' is causal where the review says 'associated with improvement'. That is defensible for pooled double-blind trials at moderate certainty, but it is the editors' choice, not the source's. The duration error below overstates how long the effect was tested.
claims.note: Not supported by this source. (1) 'During 12 to 52 weeks of treatment' is wrong for the 19-trial estimate it introduces. Figure 3 (p. 1894) gives those trials' durations as 12 weeks (17 trials), 16 weeks (1) and 24 weeks (1). The 16 trials behind the return-to-any-drinking estimate also lasted 12 to 24 weeks (Figure 2). The 12-to-52-week range is that of all 123 included studies (p. 1891). Suggested wording: 'during 12 to 24 weeks of treatment, mostly 12'. (2) 'Most participants were White men' is not in this source. The printed text gives mean age in the 40s and likely moderate-to-severe disorder, and says there was no evidence on whether benefit differs by sex or race (p. 1896). It gives no sex or race proportions (eTable 4 not read), so this detail must come from another source. Everything else from Jonas checks on the renders. Return to heavy drinking RD −0.09 (−0.13 to −0.04), 19 trials, 2875, I² 43.7%, NNT 12 (8 to 26), moderate. Crude totals recomputed from the 19 rows of Figure 3, same as the claim: 728/1593 = 45.7% against 698/1282 = 54.4%, crude difference 8.7 per 100, and 1593 + 1282 = 2875. Return to any drinking RD −0.05 (−0.10 to −0.002), 16 trials, 2347, NNT 20 (11 to 500). % drinking days −5.4 (−7.5 to −3.2); % heavy drinking days −4.1 (−7.6 to −0.61); NNH 48 (30 to 112; 17 trials, 2743), about 2 per 100. Higher oral dose 2 trials (858) and injection 2 trials (615), neither significant for return to heavy drinking. Deaths 1 against 2 (6 trials); injuries none reported; quality of life conflicting, all insufficient. Nausea, dizziness and vomiting more frequent: NNH 9, 16 and 24. The heavy-drinking threshold (4 or more drinks for women, 5 or more for men) is given on p. 1890 as the review's definition of a heavy drinking day, without a drink size in grams. The review does not say how each trial defined return to heavy drinking, so 'in most trials' cannot be checked here. Qualifiers. (a) Head to head, this review's return-to-heavy-drinking pool has 4 trials and 1141 people (RD 0.01, −0.05 to 0.06). COMBINE supplies 612 of them (54%; editors' arithmetic from Figure 3, the four trials' arms summing exactly to 1141), which supports 'more than half of the people in one US trial'. But COMBINE's naltrexone arm is the review's higher-dose group, which did not differ clearly from placebo on its own (Table 1). So the head-to-head result is mostly a comparison with that group. (b) The review notes that some trials in people not yet abstinent reported less heavy drinking with naltrexone (refs 44, 96; p. 1896). 'Uncertain' remains fair. (c) The larger injectable trial (ref 44) is first-authored by the review's last author; the conflict statement reports none. The claim gives no dose number, which is correct.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2, critically low (provisional). The domain judgments match the text, and the rating is driven by the project's strict readings of items 2 and 4 and by item 7, as the card says. Under lenient readings it would be moderate.

missed: Trial durations behind the naltrexone estimates. The 19 trials of the main oral group for return to heavy drinking lasted 12 weeks (17), 16 weeks (1) or 24 weeks (1) (Figure 3), and the 16 trials for return to any drinking 12 to 24 weeks (Figure 2). The card's can_establish ('over 12 to 52 weeks') and cannot_establish ('durability beyond 52 weeks') hold for acamprosate (12–52 weeks in Figure 2) but not for naltrexone, where the pooled evidence covers at most 24 weeks and mostly 12. The naltrexone claim repeats '12 to 52 weeks'.

Crude against pooled acamprosate effect. The crude difference in return to any drinking is 7.0 per 100 (76.4% against 83.4%), smaller than the pooled 9, because with I² 80.8% the random-effects weights give the two large US low-risk trials (COMBINE and Mason 2006) 16% of the weight for 25% of the participants and 28% of the events (editors' arithmetic from Figure 2).

COMBINE's medical management as described here: up to 9 manual-guided visits at weeks 0, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 16, about 45 then 20 minutes each (p. 1896). This is relevant to the COMBINE claim's 'nine brief medical-support visits'.
